explain.text: Dutch has two words for *the*: **de** and **het**. You can't guess which one a noun takes from English, so always learn a noun together with its article. About two in three nouns are *de*-words.
Every plural takes **de**, and every diminutive (a word ending in *-je*) takes **het**: *de stoelen*, *het stoeltje*.

Some groups help you guess. Most nouns that start with *ge-* or *be-* are **het**-words (*het gebouw*, *het bezoek*), and so are most nouns that end in *-ment*, *-isme* or *-um* (*het appartement*, *het toerisme*, *het museum*). Languages are **het** too: *het Nederlands*.
Nouns that end in *-heid*, *-ie* or the verb suffix *-ing* are almost always **de**-words: *de vrijheid*, *de familie*, *de oplossing*.

explain.nl: De fiets staat voor de deur.
explain.en: The bike is in front of the door.

explain.text: Most plurals end in **-en**: *de stoel → de stoelen*. The spelling follows the sound. A long vowel written with two letters loses one in the open syllable (*boom → bomen*), a short vowel gets a double consonant (*man → mannen*), and *s* and *f* between vowels turn into *z* and *v* (*huis → huizen*, *brief → brieven*).

explain.text: After an unstressed *-el, -em, -en, -er* or *-je* the plural is **-s**: *de tafel → de tafels*, *de bakker → de bakkers*, *het meisje → de meisjes*. Words ending in *a, i, o, u* or *y* take **'s**: *de auto → de auto's*, *de baby → de baby's*.

A handful of common nouns are irregular, so learn them as pairs: *het kind → de kinderen*, *het ei → de eieren*, *de stad → de steden*, *het schip → de schepen*, *de dag → de dagen*, *het lid → de leden*.
